title: Impact of Political Turnover on Public Spending

llm_response.content:
## 1. Identification Strategy
- Method: Instrumental Variables (2SLS). Use close-election Democratic wins (z) as an instrument for Democratic control (x) to estimate the causal effect on log public spending (y).
- Rationale: Democratic control may be endogenous (e.g., correlated with unobserved local conditions that also affect spending). Near-threshold Democratic wins are as-good-as-random, shifting x exogenously.
- Key assumptions:
  - Relevance: z affects x (first-stage is strong).
  - Exclusion: z affects y only through x, conditional on controls (no other direct channel from a narrow win to spending).
  - Independence/As-if random: Near the win threshold, assignment of z is as good as random with respect to potential outcomes.
  - Monotonicity: A close Democratic win weakly increases Democratic control (no defiers).
  - SUTVA: No interference across units.

## 2. R Code
```r
# Load or install required packages
req_pkgs <- c("AER", "sandwich", "lmtest")
for (p in req_pkgs) {
  if (!require(p, character.only = TRUE, quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages(p, repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")
    library(p, character.only = TRUE)
  }
}

# Read data
df <- read.csv("experiments/exp_b/data/s74_data.csv")

# Basic checks
stopifnot(all(c("y","x","z","controls") %in% names(df)))
df <- na.omit(df)
N <- nrow(df)

cat("Sample size (after drop NA):", N, "\n")

# OLS benchmark (potentially biased)
m_ols <- lm(y ~ x + controls, data = df)
vc_ols <- sandwich::vcovHC(m_ols, type = "HC2")
ols_ct <- lmtest::coeftest(m_ols, vcov = vc_ols)
beta_ols <- coef(m_ols)["x"]
se_ols <- sqrt(diag(vc_ols))["x"]
t_ols <- beta_ols / se_ols
p_ols <- 2 * (1 - pnorm(abs(t_ols)))

cat("\nOLS (y ~ x + controls):\n")
cat(sprintf("  beta_x = %.4f, SE = %.4f, p = %.4f\n", beta_ols, se_ols, p_ols))

# First stage: x on z and controls
m_fs <- lm(x ~ z + controls, data = df)
vc_fs <- sandwich::vcovHC(m_fs, type = "HC2")
fs_ct <- lmtest::coeftest(m_fs, vcov = vc_fs)
beta_fs_z <- coef(m_fs)["z"]
se_fs_z <- sqrt(diag(vc_fs))["z"]
t_fs_z <- beta_fs_z / se_fs_z
F_fs <- as.numeric(t_fs_z^2)

cat("\nFirst stage (x ~ z + controls):\n")
cat(sprintf("  coef[z] = %.4f, SE = %.4f, t = %.2f, robust F(z|controls) = %.2f\n",
            beta_fs_z, se_fs_z, t_fs_z, F_fs))

# Reduced form: y on z and controls
m_rf <- lm(y ~ z + controls, data = df)
vc_rf <- sandwich::vcovHC(m_rf, type = "HC2")
beta_rf_z <- coef(m_rf)["z"]
se_rf_z <- sqrt(diag(vc_rf))["z"]
t_rf_z <- beta_rf_z / se_rf_z
p_rf_z <- 2 * (1 - pnorm(abs(t_rf_z)))

cat("\nReduced form (y ~ z + controls):\n")
cat(sprintf("  coef[z] = %.4f, SE = %.4f, p = %.4f\n", beta_rf_z, se_rf_z, p_rf_z))

# 2SLS main specification
m_iv <- AER::ivreg(y ~ x + controls | z + controls, data = df)
vc_iv <- sandwich::vcovHC(m_iv, type = "HC2")
beta_iv <- coef(m_iv)["x"]
se_iv <- sqrt(diag(vc_iv))["x"]
t_iv <- beta_iv / se_iv
p_iv <- 2 * (1 - pnorm(abs(t_iv)))

cat("\nMain 2SLS (y ~ x + controls | z + controls):\n")
cat(sprintf("  beta_x(IV) = %.4f, SE = %.4f, p = %.4f\n", beta_iv, se_iv, p_iv))
cat(sprintf("  First-stage robust F(z|controls) = %.2f\n", F_fs))

# Robustness 1: Add quadratic term in controls
m_iv_q <- AER::ivreg(y ~ x + controls + I(controls^2) | z + controls + I(controls^2), data = df)
vc_iv_q <- sandwich::vcovHC(m_iv_q, type = "HC2")
beta_iv_q <- coef(m_iv_q)["x"]
se_iv_q <- sqrt(diag(vc_iv_q))["x"]
t_iv_q <- beta_iv_q / se_iv_q
p_iv_q <- 2 * (1 - pnorm(abs(t_iv_q)))

cat("\nRobustness #1 (add quadratic in controls):\n")
cat(sprintf("  beta_x(IV) = %.4f, SE = %.4f, p = %.4f\n", beta_iv_q, se_iv_q, p_iv_q))

# Robustness 2: Trim outliers in y (1% tails)
lo <- quantile(df$y, 0.01, na.rm = TRUE)
hi <- quantile(df$y, 0.99, na.rm = TRUE)
df_trim <- subset(df, y >= lo & y <= hi)
m_iv_trim <- AER::ivreg(y ~ x + controls | z + controls, data = df_trim)
vc_iv_trim <- sandwich::vcovHC(m_iv_trim, type = "HC2")
beta_iv_trim <- coef(m_iv_trim)["x"]
se_iv_trim <- sqrt(diag(vc_iv_trim))["x"]
t_iv_trim <- beta_iv_trim / se_iv_trim
p_iv_trim <- 2 * (1 - pnorm(abs(t_iv_trim)))

# Also report first-stage F in trimmed sample
m_fs_trim <- lm(x ~ z + controls, data = df_trim)
vc_fs_trim <- sandwich::vcovHC(m_fs_trim, type = "HC2")
se_fs_z_trim <- sqrt(diag(vc_fs_trim))["z"]
t_fs_z_trim <- coef(m_fs_trim)["z"] / se_fs_z_trim
F_fs_trim <- as.numeric(t_fs_z_trim^2)

cat("\nRobustness #2 (trim 1% tails of y):\n")
cat(sprintf("  beta_x(IV) = %.4f, SE = %.4f, p = %.4f, N = %d\n",
            beta_iv_trim, se_iv_trim, p_iv_trim, nrow(df_trim)))
cat(sprintf("  First-stage robust F(z|controls) [trimmed] = %.2f\n", F_fs_trim))

# Final printed summary
cat("\nSummary:\n")
cat(sprintf("  Main 2SLS beta_x = %.4f (SE = %.4f, p = %.4f), N = %d\n",
            beta_iv, se_iv, p_iv, N))
cat(sprintf("  First-stage robust F = %.2f (rule-of-thumb > 10 for strong IV)\n", F_fs))
cat("  OLS beta_x (for comparison) =", sprintf("%.4f", beta_ols), "\n")
```

## 3. Expected Findings
- Sign: Positive. Democratic control is typically associated with higher public spending; the LATE identified by close-election wins should reflect this.
- Magnitude: In logs, a one-unit increase in the Democratic control index (x) is expected to raise log spending by roughly 0.05 to 0.15. If x were a binary switch from non-Democratic to Democratic control, this would correspond to about a 5%–15% increase in spending. The exact scale depends on how x is normalized in the data; with the observed range roughly within [-1, 1], a 0.5 increase in x would imply about a 2.5%–7.5% increase in spending.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: Use close-election Democratic wins as an instrument for Democratic control.
_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: The analysis suggests a negative causal impact of Democratic control on public spending.
